etymologies.etymologyHTML: Partly from Latin affectionatus, partly from affection + -ate. Doublet of aficionado.

definitions.definition: (of a person) Having affection or warm regard; loving; fond.
(of an action, etc.) Characterised by or proceeding from affection; indicating love; tender.

quote.citation: 1900, Charles W[addell] Chesnutt, chapter I, in The House Behind the Cedars, Boston, Mass.; New York, N.Y.: Houghton, Mifflin and Company […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Warwick left the undertaker's shop and retraced his steps until he had passed the lawyer's office, toward which he threw an affectionate glance.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Eager; passionate; strongly inclined toward something.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Either from the adjective, or from affection + -ate (modelled on Middle French affectionner).

definitions.definition: (rare) To show affection to; to have affection for.

quote.text: Plutarch saith fitly of those who affectionate themselves to Monkies and little Dogges, that […].

quote.citation: 1721, John Rushworth, Historical Collections Of Private Passages of State, etc.: 1618—1629, volume 1, page 222:
quote.text: And firſt, his Majeſty would have you to underſtand, That there was never any King more loving to his People, or better affectionated to the right uſe of Parliaments, than his Majeſty hath approved himſelf to be, […].

quote.citation: 1838 February 1, Charles Dickens, To Catherine Dickens, 2012, Jenny Hartley (editor), The Selected Letters of Charles Dickens, page 41,
quote.text:
Ever my dear Kate your affectionated husband
CHARLES DICKENS
